title: The Brooklyn Bridge
objective: After this level you can explain how the Brooklyn Bridge was built.
summary: Caissons dug out under compressed air gave workers the bends. John Roebling designed the bridge; Washington directed it by telescope, Emily relayed his orders. It opened in 1883 on steel cables.

cards.headline: The Brooklyn Bridge's chief engineer watched it rise through a telescope.
cards.body: From his bedroom window in Brooklyn, Washington Roebling followed work he could no longer visit. How did the man in charge end up stuck at home? The answer starts at the bottom of the East River.

cards.headline: Digging from inside a box
cards.body: The bridge's two towers stand on caissons: huge bottomless boxes sunk to the riverbed. Compressed air was pumped in to keep the water out, and inside, workers dug away the sediment so the box sank deeper. Then the caissons were filled with concrete to become the towers' foundations. It's like pushing an upside-down cup into a bath: the trapped air keeps the inside dry.

cards.headline: The bends, and a family business
cards.body: Coming up too fast from that pressurized air let nitrogen bubbles form in the workers' blood: caisson disease, now called the bends. In 1872 it struck Washington Roebling. He had taken over from his father, John A. Roebling, the bridge's designer, who died of tetanus in 1869 after a ferry crushed his toes. So Washington watched through his telescope, and his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, carried his directions to the engineers on the bridge.

cards.fact: 1883: the longest span in the world, hung on steel.
cards.context: The bridge opened on May 24, 1883. Its 486-meter (1,595-foot) main span was the longest in the world when it opened, and it was the first bridge to use steel for its cable wire. It's a suspension bridge, so that deck hangs from cables in tension. Emily Roebling rode in the first carriage across, carrying a rooster as a symbol of victory.

questions.prompt: Match each Roebling with their part in building the Brooklyn Bridge.
questions.explanation: John A. Roebling was the bridge's designer. His son Washington took over and, after the bends, watched through his telescope. Emily Warren Roebling carried his directions to the engineers.

questions.prompt: What caused the caisson disease that struck Brooklyn Bridge workers?

options.label: Breathing concrete dust inside the sunken boxes
options.rationale: The illness came from pressure, not dust.

options.label: Nitrogen bubbles in the blood after leaving compressed air
Cold river water leaking into the caissons
options.rationale: Compressed air kept the water out.

options.label: Tetanus from injuries on the ferry
options.rationale: Tetanus killed John Roebling; it isn't caisson disease.

questions.explanation: Workers breathed compressed air in the caissons; coming up too fast let nitrogen bubbles form in their blood.

questions.prompt: The Brooklyn Bridge's deck hangs from steel cables that, as Level 51 showed for suspension bridges, are in _____.

options.label: compression: they're squeezed
options.rationale: Towers are squeezed; hanging cables are stretched.

options.label: no force at all
options.rationale: The cables carry the deck's weight to the towers.

options.label: bending, like a beam
options.rationale: Bending is how a beam works.

questions.explanation: In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from cables in tension, which pass the load to the towers and anchorages.
